parsedVerdict.reasoning: Both services deal with appointments, so the concern is broadly shared. What breaks the unit is that they don't use the same abstractions. SchedulingService works through the module's established pattern: it reads data through the injected DAOs (PatientDao, AppointmentDao), turns rows into domain entities (Appointment, Patient, Practitioner) that hold the invariants (overlaps, cancel, isMinor, treatsMinors), and reports failures as SchedulingError. VisitNotesService skips all of this. It calls the raw PrismaService ORM client directly (prisma.visitNote.create/findMany), builds a note as an ad-hoc VisitNote interface with no domain entity behind it, and handles its own rules inline: id format, text trimming, sorting by date. It never checks through AppointmentDao or the Appointment entity that the appointment exists, so an unknown appointmentId is never reported as SchedulingError('unknown'), unlike in SchedulingService. The module therefore has two different ways of handling persistence and domain logic. This is a bypass of the module's own abstractions, not an import-direction issue, because both files depend on the persistence layer but at different levels of abstraction. There is also a smaller point: SchedulingService maps an appointment row to an Appointment entity in two places (book and cancel) instead of in one shared mapper.

violations.message: Skips the module's abstractions: it calls PrismaService (prisma.visitNote.create/findMany) directly instead of using a DAO, and returns an ad-hoc VisitNote interface instead of a domain entity. Rules (id format, trimming, sorting) are written inline, and it never confirms the appointment exists through AppointmentDao/Appointment or reports a missing one as SchedulingError, unlike SchedulingService.
Minor: the row-to-Appointment entity mapping (new Appointment(a.id, ..., a.status as AppointmentStatus)) is repeated in book() and cancel() instead of being kept in one mapper.
